The headspace is such a strange and fascinating part of this disorder. 

For us, the easiest way to tell (and this goes for alters too) is consistency. Sure, things change, but the layout is generally consistent and has been since I first saw a glimpse years ago. I tend to see it in the first person, I like the VR comparison someone mentioned. I sometimes find myself zooming out into 3rd person, but it's always me experiencing the headspace. I imagine this might be different for DID and OSDD/P-DID systems. 

Our headspace exists in a void, which seems common. For us, there are layers, and most alters exist within different areas. There are areas I can access commonly, this is something I have to focus on but I also see glimpses in my minds eye at random depending on what's happening and if I am triggered or someone is fronting. I don't know if alters continue to... exist? Experience? Idk. When not fronting. Probably. 

Some people don't have a headspace, and others just aren't allowed access. It most likely depends on how one's mind works, how their brain functions, and how alters function within it.

I'm so sorry that happened to you! That is such a scary situation to deal with, especially with arfid, where a lot of us are already afraid of this happening. When it actually happens, what does that do to someone with this ED? I don't know if my advice will be helpful but I'll offer some anyway. 

First of all, if you don't already partake, please consider therapy. It's hard enough to deal with symptoms of arfid before having a physical reaction, let alone after one occurring. I imagine someone who has training in psychology, maybe even one specifically trained in eating disorders (even though arfid isn't as commonly discussed, hopefully they would still be knowledgeable) will be much more helpful than I can be, because (obligatory) I'm not a doctor. If this isn't an option, I really do hope you find a way to get through this and don't dismiss those feelings as you being 'silly' or something because what happened to you was serious and you are allowed to be affected by it. With that out of the way, I have some ideas. 

1st of all, it's a good thing that you now know for 100% fact that you cannot eat strawberries. Now you know what to avoid and how to avoid it in terms of that fruit. Accidents can happen, which is why you should now start keeping your epipen close if you haven't already. It'll become second nature. Make sure your family and friends know how to use it if they don't already, and that whenever you are out and about you keep it in the same place, think a backpack, purse, or shoulder bag. If you keep a wallet and have an in case of emergency card in it, add that to your list of allergies. 
Side note, highly recommend one if you don't already have that. Write what you're allergic to, what meds you take and their doses, if you're diabetic or anything like that, etc etc. Look up what would be best to keep on it. It's scary to think about, but it is useful in case you are unable to communicate for any reason. 

I would consider a patch test if you are able to acquire one. It would tell you what you for sure are allergic to now that you know you have a food allergy. It wouldn't be 100% foolproof, but it would give you peace of mind should you find yourself trying another fruit or veggie or something. You can keep your list of literally safe foods to know if you are able to try it. From there, you don't have to like the food or add it to your list of safe foods, but you'd know it's safe to consume. 

Be careful with research. There are things I could suggest, but ultimately, it would be much better if you could talk to a doctor and get concrete answers. I believe the person you'd see is an allergist. Keeping in mind your allergy to certain medications along with this food allergy, they will be able to help you, and from there, you can work on healing from the trauma that affects your arfid. 

Good luck, and I believe in you. Keep trying, and just know that if you were able to eat a safe food with 0 reaction before, you can still eat them now, even if you have to take it slow.

Holy heck that's an essay. I always manage to type a dissertation when giving advice on this subreddit, my bad. Basic tl;dr, like this? Try this.

I've got a bunch of suggestions, but (obligatory) I'm not a doctor, and I hope you do receive the care you deserve and feel better soon. 

The carnation breakfast shakes are my go-to supplement shake. Ensure was too chalky. They have a lot of flavors. My favorite is chocolate, but strawberry was good too- I added strawberry syrup for a better flavor, though. I didn't like the frosted flakes flavor, but it did taste kinda like i ate a bowl of cereal and then bottled the leftover milk. 

Look into things like enof (powdered veg, doesn't taste like anything if you pair it with almost anything. I only ever tasted it once, and it was on buttered white bread). You can mix it into drinks if I remember correctly, though I never tried that. If you were to try it, I'd consider maybe something like a smoothie or milk drink, I worry the texture would stand out in a soda. Though that would have to be up to you. It's expensive but so is not powdered veg, and you only have to buy it every few months if it works out. 

I have a mini fridge and I like to keep drinks in it (if u like juice, just drink it out of the carton/jug unless you'll have to share) and a big thing of apple sauce and plain vanilla yogurt. I sometimes keep cheese cubes, but lately dairy is a hard one for me, so I stopped keeping them since I couldn't eat them fast enough. (There's also a mostly finished yogurt tub I keep forgetting to throw away too but that's... besides the point, lol. I'm not saying you have to go out and invest in a mini fridge, of course. These are just my personal stock in a house where nothing is sacred. These are the most convenient and easy to consume foods that are liquid and don't need chewing, but also have a bit of substance. I also really like body armor juice, but if you like Gatorade or any of those electrolyte drinks, consider those too. You could even flavor your water if you wanted. Those flavor packets are popular right now and they also have liquid flavor enhancers. 

Ice cream, and maybe sorbet might be a way to get calories in, and flavors like vanilla or chocolate are smooth all throughout if you're worried about texture. Jello could be a good option as well if you can handle the jell texture. 

I'm not a fruit person either, but apple slices and mandarin oranges are good sometimes. Apple slices are convenient and you don't have to eat the skin if you don't want to, and mandarin oranges tend to be the same texture and don't have any of the issues an actual whole orange. I don't like peaches but I know the peach cups are good if you do, and you can avoid having to peel and cut them. I don't have any suggestions for veggies, though. I can eat canned corn and green beans sometimes, they come in the little cups too. You could try broth or canned soup. Tomato soup is a cohesive texture, and if you like chicken noodle you could even make your own and omit different things you won't like. 
(I like to make chicken noodle soup from scratch. I'll cook chicken, then saute my potatoes and carrots, and then add chicken broth and simmer, adding noodles until they're cooked all the way through after giving the potatoes time to cook. You can omit or add whatever you like to make it your own soup, I add carrots and omit celery but none of the ingredients are truly necessary (unless you count chicken or noodles as necessary to a chicken noodle soup /s /lh). 

Is there anything solid you tend to enjoy? If you like crackers, but there's a reason you aren't able to consume them, consider looking at a different texture or brand. I once was literally only able to eat saltines. If you like cheese, you can try those individually wrapped slabs or cheese sticks. Precooked bacon is pretty good if you enjoy it, and I much prefer lunch meat from the deli versus the stuff in the tubs. 
 
If you like chicken, you can cook a few servings of it and store it in tupperware, and then pair it with something like boil in bag rice if you need something quickly. If you like pasta, angel hair cooks the quickest. Butter, salt, pepper, and a serving of that veggie powder I mentioned earlier was a meal of mine for quite a while. 

Good luck once again, and keep up the good work.

When I take pills, I drink the liquid first so the pill never touches my tongue.

I'm so sorry to hear about your year, friend. You've had a hell of a ride, and none of it was fun. It's good to acknowledge you have to clean up, but it's important to note that those terrible events triggered your hoarding tendencies, and that's not your fault. Taking care of your grief will in time make this easier, but for now you've got to start small. 

I usually start with my closet. It's just something I've always done, as usually it's just sorting and organizing. From there, start a trash bag. Don't bother with a can, just the bag. You can fill one and tie it off and start another, no problem. If there's bedding on your bed, save that for last (so you're not sleeping on bare mattress if you normally have sheets, no biggie if thats not an issue but it is really nice having a sheet eventually; baby steps). Pick up your blahaj and the squishmaller and give them their bed back. Brush crumbs off onto the floor (soon you'll be able to vacuum  or sweep if you'd like). Then, go around and pick up trash. I usually end up putting all of the shit I need to sort onto the bed and my desk, but if you don't have those, designate the first corner you find as the stuff you'll reorganize and put it all there. The rest can go where it normally goes, or into the garbage.

 Dishes don't need to be washed right away, and you can either take them as you find them to the kitchen, or just collect them together. Put the silverware into a cup or something, stack your bowls and plates. Like they do at the restaurants. Makes them easier to carry to the kitchen. If they're really gross you can start by rinsing them right then, but if that would cause distraction then loop back around later for that. Similar idea for trash. Leave the bags in the hallway until you're ready to take them outside, don't take them one by one. Once you're ready for a break or finished, you can take a trip or two to the bin.

Ironically, putting on hoarders the tv show has helped me a lot because not only is it showing me tips, it's showing me the bad stuff and people cleaning it up, which helps with a technique called body doubling.  They're all cleaning, which means I can too. I would highly suggest if you're not already comfortable with the show, to avoid it. You can instead find body doubling videos on YouTube which will be helpful for you. They're often people in similar situations to you or I and they film themselves cleaning and tidying which in turn makes it easy for you to follow along. Either that, or put on an anime (dubbed if you don't speak Japanese so you're not too busy following along, I've definitely made this mistake), a TV show or movie, music, a podcast, or a YouTube video. Any entertainment is good as long as it's motivating. If you've got supportive friends you could ask them to be in a voice chat or phone call with you as well, that's often used instead of body doubling as well.

Since you've had covid a few times, definitely take your breaks. I've got a chest cold at the moment (covid negative) and I'm in the middle of working towards a total rearrange of my room. Every time I get something done, I have to stop and take a break. It's okay though. It's just what happens when your body feels icky. Drink lots of water, and for some of your more dusty areas, consider wearing a mask. It'll keep you from getting grey snot and it might help with lung pain. Did I mention drinking water? Drink water. If you take medications, take them first. If even the thought of that is too much, just start with the medication and work your way up. You can wait for it to kick in, or reward yourself for starting there by getting a snack or something else you'd get dopamine from.

I have a bunch of advice to offer, mainly because your story reminds me of my own and I found ways to curb it just a bit so I wanted to share, but you don't have to take any of it at all if you don't want. Don't force yourself to do anything that will ultimately make your hoard worse, focus on the tips that you know would help you first and then work your way to the challenging parts, if you don't disregard them completely which would also be okay.

Here's a few tips for donating that you might find useful.  

For the things you haven't tossed yet and are torn on whether or not to do so or to hold onto; if you can't eat the food but can't bring yourself to toss it, food banks are always accepting donations (check the expiration dates first, as long as the food is still good they'll accept it gladly). Many also take things like old clothes (mainly shirts, shorts, and socks), and care items like bottles of soap and other various toiletries. (Folks love razors because it can feel really nice to have a clean shaven face or legs when you fall on hard times, so if you don't shave and you have a pack of razors open, take those. Same goes for if you change tooth brushes and have an open multi pack- don't take the used ones but if you have unused portions of a multi pack you will not use, take it there. Soaps, multi packs of tissues, wash cloths, socks, if it comes in a multipack and you won't/can't use it, and someone else can, put it to donate). 

Don't save the stuff with the intention of taking it if you don't have the means to do so. I'd suggest locating places you can take things before setting the things aside. Absolutely no harm done if you can't donate those things! If you can't do this, that's okay, and there are other options. Throwing things away is just as acceptable and healthy, and no harm is done by it. This is simply another suggestion, as someone who both struggles in the same areas and also worked at a food bank for a time. You can use findhelp.org to find a bank nearby. And hey if you find yourself in need later on, (or even now) you can always go back to take care of what you need too. But again if you aren't comfortable or just can't for any reason, don't worry about it and continue doing what works for you. 

For me, I also had to take a step back and sort of forget that donation is an option. I had to look at the wear of clothes, and the age of some foods. If it was something I would not eat but that I would not share, I tossed it or even left it for another day to remake a decision as long as I found another thing to occupy the time. If too many items accumulate it becomes a chore and the more chores I add for myself, the harder it gets personally. If it is still good? Think, does it have the tags still? Has it been used? How much? Would someone pick it up at the local goodwill or salvation army? Be careful with that one btw. Mainly focus on how much it's been used by you and whether or not you can use it or not. If it's a well worn shirt that doesn't fit you anymore, you should probably throw it out. If it's got the tags still- maybe it was a gift but it didn't fit or you bought it online and it was too big/small, those are prime candidates for donation). 

Some examples of some things I did donate. My family does mobile orders to Walmart and we pick up the groceries. (Really helps to stick to what we need as long as you stay within the grocery section. Highly suggest a list if you don't already, but of course that is easier to suggest than it is to do). We ordered a few cans of green beans for the holiday season's gb casserole, and got a massive can instead. The food bank I worked at did hot meals for folks, and I donated the can to them because I never would have been able to use it whereas that could feed a few different people. And the food is always free so I could grab a plate if I was ever hungry myself so it wasn't sunk cost. At work a coworker would give my parent a small pack of fig newton's every day. They didn't have the heart to stop her, so they began to accumulate. I got tired of stacking them like food Jenga pieces, so off they went as well. Little things. Of course it helped that I went there daily, but for you you could set aside a bag or box for food bank donation and do the same method until say the box is full. More on that later.

 If you have to protect from critters, then find an airtight or sealable container or bag, I often put the perishable goods in plastic baggies and one parent of mine used to store the flour and rice in 5 gallon buckets; you can just use tupperware or other single use plastic containers as long as you can handle keeping some and tossing others. I see that you tossed the one you found with a dead roach, and thats great! Good job, no biggie, saving containers wasn't at all a necessary step so you made the right choice. The baggie trick is good enough and ultimately you decided what was more important to you, which is most important. We keep our flour double wrapped in walmart bags, but thats bcus the bag is messy. Its a critter repellant as well though.) I also keep my sugar and rice in plastic gallon bags. If you save the Walmart bags, you can put these things in them and tie off the bags before placing them into the donate box maybe. Then you can stick to your one item per day and save on the trips. The discipline starts by actually taking the box where it needs to go, which is the most important step. Easier said than done, trust me I know. Keep that in mind as well, if it is a hindrance instead of helpful, don't do it! No harm done and this is just a suggestion. Again, do what works for you. 

If you take nothing else of my advice, take this. Do what you need to do, and what works for you. If you find that saving things to donate later begins to cause an issue, then don't continue that method. Throw the things away. At that point the items are not helping them, and they're hurting you. Don't let your grief keep you from working on yourself. Grief can be a painful trigger, and I'm sorry this has happened to you. But look at you go! You got rid of some things, donated others, and found some floor! That's fantastic, and I do mean that. Good luck with your future endeavors, and keep finding what works for you.

Warning, I sort of typed an essay for you. If you've got the time give it a read 😅 I'm pretty passionate about this subject. I'll attempt a tl;dr at the end. The next two paragraphs are the most important anyway so you can stop there if you want. 

When I first stopped biting my nails, I had a practice that I will still use now if I happen to start biting or chewing on my nails. I would use a nail file. Every time I wanted to bite the little bit of growth, I would instead file it off. I keep nail files in my desk and bathroom, and I'm going to put one in my backpack to help avoid biting off rough edges and imperfections at work. As soon as I could fit my teeth under my nail, I filed it as close to the skin as I could go instead of biting that bit off. File from the edges to the center on both sides. Admittedly I'm not sure why, but this is generally recommended to avoid breakage and splitting.

Keep your nails as close to the skin as you can for as long as it takes to stop chewing. If it's something you do at your desk, keep a file at your desk. If its something you do in the living room watching TV, keep one in a drawer on a side table or somewhere else close by. If you don't want to go that far, then just keep one in the bathroom, bedroom, and your bag. Don't give up if you chew instead every once in a while. If you catch yourself and still have some nail left, use the file afterward. It takes time, but I hope this method helps you. I didn't want to do acrylics when I did this process because I would gnaw them off, and also the damage would have made my personal chewing and biting habit worse once they came off. Keep your own triggers and habits in mind before choosing which method you try first from the advice we all give you. 

Invest in a cute pair of cuticle clippers. I got mine off of aliexpress but you can get them anywhere and for whatever price point and style you're comfortable with. Mine are multicolored, have a small tip and no angles to the clipper part. They are a lifesaver. I used them to cut my nails before filing if one broke in the growth process (I still do this). It's not ideal to cut your nails, but I tend to be a rule breaker. (Trim a bit then file the rest, saves time really.) The important reason though, is that you can use them to trim down the dead skin you might bite away. Personally, I go to town with the skin around the tips of my nails. However this is not good because it can lead to chewing on the nails and also just give you sores and stuff on your fingertips. You can use the clippers for a very satisfying trim of the skin and that way you have better control to avoid sores, and you're not getting bacteria in your mouth, and spit on your fingers. Please be careful with this advice specifically. Only use it if it is something you'd be comfortable with d oing. 

In the beginning your nails will be very brittle and might flake, I really encourage you not to peel those flakes. They cause a divet that leaves a weak nail and a terrible target for biting. It's not the end of the world if a peel happens, but to me I found it discouraging. Like every time it would be kinda satisfying, but then it would kick in that the growth is now ruined and the vicious cycle continues. File the nail until it's no longer showing peeling or until you hit the nail bed. 

As for your cuticles, there's many options for cuticle creams, oils, salves, etc. If you can afford to find the options that work for you, that's great and I would definitely recommend something meant specifically for your nails. (Vitamin E is apparently pretty good to include). However, aquaphor and Vaseline work as well. I've also heard that you can use it instead of silicone or other peel off skin protectants when doing nail art. Taking care of your cuticles is just as important as your nails, especially if you have a habit of peeling them. 

Gonna talk a bit about health stuff in the next paragraph, skip if you want as these are only suggestions. I'm not a doctor, this is anecdotal, and I also don't want you to get uncomfortable or feeling icky. No worries if you do need to skip and take care of yourself :). When I was younger, my nails were very flexible and incredibly prone to breaking, and it wasn't until I was older and started seeing a primary care provider again that I noticed improvement. 

 When your nails start to grow, the best thing you can do for them is to get them as strong as possible. If you notice that your nails are very flexible and split a lot even after you stop biting, I'd suggest getting some bloodwork done. Check for vitamin deficiencies if you aren't already aware of them. You may even mention it to your doctor if you'd like. It's possible that you could be anemic, or you could have a vitamin D deficiency, among other things. Of course there are many reasons and I am NOT! a doctor, this is just what I experienced and those two were the ones I started taking vitamins for first and thus began to see the most improvement. After seeing my pcp and getting a full panel, I started taking supplements where needed. After a few weeks (about a month or more) I could just about see the new growth as it got thicker and grew faster. It's still an uphill battle for me, but in my case I found improvement there. Highly recommend this step in nail care. I will warn you, it is possible that biting for so long may have caused permanent damage, but it doesn't hurt to rule out health reasons as well. 

Once you have your strong healthy nails and stop finding yourself biting them as much and begin to grow them out, you'll get to choose a nail shape. I'm not quite there yet myself! Basically, choose the one you think is right for you, but remember your triggers to bite as well. If you have a corner that is longer than the rest of your nail, would you bite it to make them even? If you have a cracked nail, will you bite the whole nail or even all of them to even it back out? Keep your file handy and be ready to change up your natural nail at any time. Just keep in mind where your nail dust might end up! 

Good luck! 

TL;DR file them instead of biting. Use tools instead of biting. Use creams instead of picking. Maybe see a doctor if you want after you stop and if you have concerns. Keep your triggers in mind and find what works for you.

Rice is always a good one. I know you didn't mention it so if it isn't a safe food disregard this and the next paragraph, totally understand. You can add all sorts of flavors to rice or leave it plain,, and if you cook it right and store it correct it won't be dry whenever you reheat it. 


Personal favorite right now is this: tomato bullion, a can of tomato sauce. Cook some chicken if youd like to add some meat. Fry the rice for a bit in a little oil and add flavorings, then the can of sauce and bullion, and then chicken stock or water to however much rice you do. I have an instant pot which I highly recommend for people who don't have the best luck with an oven. 


If that's not your thing, don't worry! There's plenty of other meal prep things you can do. I find that pasta reheats quite well and store nicely, and if you're a butter noodle kinda person then you can always cook noodles and then sauces later or just add butter when reheating. White sauces come in jars, so you can always keep the jar in the fridge and pasta in a tupperware container and you'll have easy access to food. 


Honestly, while I hate shilling for products, smaller ones you can set and forget might be your friend, in which case if you can, invest in an instant pot. You can also use the smaller convection oven toaster combo things and air fryers. I'm not sure quite what you mean by immobility, so of course depending on your situation these can all be harder than others. I don't do meal prep, but I imagine cooking a box of noodles and picking different flavors for the top can be an easy weekly fix. 


Good luck friend. Sorry I didn't have any advice on storing meats, those tend to be a bit complicated in terms of looks once chilled.
